note: One record for all 110 attributes on the wheel. The beginner definition is the Descriptor Golf clue, so it must describe the attribute WITHOUT using any word from its own label, or the hole becomes a word search against a wheel that already shows every name - buildAttributes throws on a clue that leaks, and a test covers it. The expert definition carries the diagnostic detail a Q candidate needs, and repeatedly names what an attribute is confused with and why. Intensity anchors are deliberately absent: a calibrated 0-15 value is panel measurement data against a physical kit, not something that can be written from a desk.

definition.beginner: Character created by the heat of the drum rather than anything the bean brought from the farm: smoke, char, toast, and the edge of burning.
definition.expert: Pyrolytic attributes generated during roasting. Increases with development time and drum temperature, progressively masking origin character.

causes.note: Rises steadily with development; dominant past second crack.

definition.beginner: Sweetened cured leaf — the aroma of an unlit pouch rather than anything alight: soft, honeyed, faintly woody.
definition.expert: Cased and sweetened cured leaf. Distinguished from its unsweetened neighbour by the honeyed top note and softer, less dusty body.

definition.beginner: Dry cured leaf without any sweetening: dusty, slightly bitter, the smell of a fresh cigarette before it is lit.
definition.expert: Unsweetened cured leaf. Frequently confused with aged or old-crop woodiness, which arrives from storage rather than from the roast.

references.name: Unsmoked pipe tobacco or a cigar leaf, from a tobacconist
references.prep: A pinch in a covered cup, smelled unlit. Unlit is the whole reference - anything burning has moved to smoky.

causes.note: Often reported in aged or long-stored lots as well as darker roasts.

definition.beginner: Past the point of pleasant browning: sharp, dark, carbonised.
definition.expert: Carbonisation attributes beyond the sugar-browning range. A fault when it dominates, though light smoke is stylistic in some dark blends.

causes.note: Excess drum temperature or development past second crack.

definition.beginner: Dry toasted grain-and-husk character, like a breakfast box or a plain cracker.
definition.expert: Toasted starch attributes. Under-development pushes this toward raw and dusty; adequate development pushes it toward sweetness.

causes.note: Prominent in under-developed roasts where starches have toasted but sugars have not caramelised.

definition.beginner: Sharp and stinging at the back of the throat — the pungent bite of something scorched.
definition.expert: Trigeminal irritation from over-carbonisation. Perceived as a physical sting rather than an aroma, which separates it from its dry, powdery neighbour.

causes.note: Scorching from excessive charge temperature or a stalled, then rushed, roast.

definition.beginner: Dry, powdery and cold, like a fireplace the morning after.
definition.expert: Residual carbon character. Distinguished from the stinging neighbour by being drying and inert rather than pungent.

references.name: Cold ash from a wood fire or a charcoal grill
references.prep: A teaspoon of cold, dry ash in a covered cup. It must be cold and it must be dry: warm ash smells of smoke, which is a different attribute one wedge away.

causes.note: Surface carbonisation, often alongside oil migration to the bean surface.

definition.beginner: Wood-fire aroma clinging to clothing — drying on the palate rather than sharp.
definition.expert: Phenolic-adjacent wood combustion character. Stylistic at low intensity in dark blends; at high intensity it is indistinguishable from a roast fault.

references.name: Lapsang souchong tea, dry leaf
references.prep: Smell the dry leaf, then steep 2 g in 100 ml of water just off the boil for three minutes and smell the surface. Pine-smoked tea is the cleanest single-note smoke available in a kitchen.

references.name: Smoked paprika (pimenton de la Vera)
references.prep: A quarter teaspoon in a covered cup. Warm it briefly in the hand first - the aroma is slow to leave a cold powder.

causes.note: Also introduced by exhaust or chaff burning in a poorly maintained roaster.

definition.beginner: The comfortable middle of sugar caramelisation in the drum: toasted, deep and rounded, with no char and no rawness.
definition.expert: The desirable centre of the sugar-browning range. The reference point against which under-development and carbonisation are both judged.

causes.note: The target zone for most commercial roast profiles.

definition.beginner: Dry, plain and husky, like uncooked oats or the smell inside a flour bag.
definition.expert: Raw starch character with no sweetness developed. A reliable marker of under-development, and easily mistaken for staling.

references.name: Unsweetened puffed wheat or plain toasted wheat cereal
references.prep: Crush a tablespoon coarsely, cover for five minutes, then smell. Buy the unsweetened one: added sugar drags the reference toward caramel and away from the point.

causes.note: Insufficient development time; the classic under-roast signature.

definition.beginner: Toasted grain with sweetness behind it, like the crust of a fresh loaf or a milkshake powder.
definition.expert: Toasted starch with caramelisation present. The sweet counterpart to plain toasted starch, and a sign that development was adequate.

references.name: Malted barley drink powder - Horlicks, Ovaltine, or dry malt extract from a brewing supplier
references.prep: A heaped teaspoon of the dry powder in a covered cup. Smell it dry first, then add 30 ml of warm water and smell again - the wet smell is the one that turns up in coffee.

causes.note: Appears once development is sufficient to caramelise sugars alongside the starches.

definition.beginner: Two families that sit together: the oily toasted character of shelled kernels, and the dry bitterness of ground beans.
definition.expert: Maillard-derived attributes spanning kernel and confection character. The most commonly reported category in commercial blends, and the one beginners over-use.

definition.beginner: Oily, toasted, mildly sweet kernel character — the smell of a warm shell being cracked.
definition.expert: Toasted kernel attributes. Shares Maillard aromatics with toasted starch, which is why the boundary with cereal is a genuine judgement call.

definition.beginner: Dry, dark, faintly bitter powder — the smell of a baking tin rather than a sweet bar.
definition.expert: Unsweetened confection character, largely a roast artefact. Where roast ends and this begins is a matter of judgement rather than fact.

definition.beginner: The dusty, skin-on, faintly savoury kernel you find in a bar snack bowl.
definition.expert: Legume rather than true kernel character: drier and more savoury than the others in this group, with a papery skin note.

references.name: Roasted unsalted peanuts, skins on
references.prep: Crush three or four nuts and cover for two minutes. Salted nuts confound the basic-taste reference with the aroma one.

definition.beginner: Sweet, buttery and slightly floral kernel — the base of a chocolate spread.
definition.expert: The sweetest and most aromatic of the kernel group, with a distinct lactonic roundness the others lack.

references.name: Shelled hazelnuts, raw
references.prep: Crush two nuts and cover for two minutes. Hazelnut spread will not do - it is mostly sugar and cocoa.

definition.beginner: Blanched, faintly bitter kernel with a marzipan edge.
definition.expert: Benzaldehyde-adjacent character. The driest of the kernel group and the one most often confused with toasted starch.

references.name: Blanched raw almonds
references.prep: Crush two nuts and cover. Keep a roasted almond alongside: the pair separates the nut from the roast, which is the confusion the wheel places two wedges apart.

definition.beginner: Sweetened, milky and rounded confection character.
definition.expert: Sweetened confection with dairy roundness. Separated from its darker sibling by sweetness and lower drying bitterness.

references.name: Unsweetened cocoa powder, not drinking chocolate
references.prep: A teaspoon in a covered cup. Check the label for added sugar or milk solids; either one turns the reference into a confectionery smell.

definition.beginner: High-percentage confection: drying, bitter, with little sweetness to soften it.
definition.expert: Unsweetened to high-percentage confection with pronounced astringency. Substantially a roast artefact in coffee rather than an origin character.

references.name: Plain dark chocolate, 85% cocoa solids or higher
references.prep: Break a square, let it sit covered for five minutes at room temperature, then smell. Taste it too: this attribute carries bitterness that cocoa powder alone does not.

causes.note: Deepens with development; at the far end it becomes indistinguishable from roast character.

definition.beginner: Not sugar on the tongue but the aromas the brain reads as sugary: syrup, cooked sugar, soft baking notes.
definition.expert: Aromatic sweetness rather than the basic taste. On the cupping form this is scored as an attribute in its own right, distinct from perceived intensity of the basic taste.

definition.beginner: Cooked syrup with dark, faintly mineral depth — what unrefined cane smells like.
definition.expert: Caramelisation products with molasses depth. The group where roast-derived and origin-derived sweetness are hardest to separate.

definition.beginner: Warm, creamy, faintly floral pod character with real complexity behind it.
definition.expert: Natural pod extract: complex, with floral and lactonic facets absent from the isolated compound.

references.name: A whole vanilla pod
references.prep: Split the pod lengthways and smell the seeds and the inner wall. Keep it in a sealed jar between sessions; it stays useful for years.

definition.beginner: The single flat note of a synthesised compound: sugary, one-dimensional, like cheap ice cream.
definition.expert: The isolated compound. Reads as a single note where the natural extract reads as a chord - the distinction is complexity, not intensity.

references.name: Synthetic vanilla essence, labelled vanillin or vanilla flavouring
references.prep: One drop on a strip of filter paper, smelled after ten seconds. Smell it against a real pod in the same session - that pair is the lesson, and neither one teaches it alone.

definition.beginner: A general impression of sugariness with no particular source you can name.
definition.expert: An umbrella impression used when the sweetness carries no identifiable character. Frequently a hedge - worth pushing a taster to specify.

definition.beginner: The umbrella smell of baking: sugar, dairy and warm spice together, none dominant.
definition.expert: A compound impression rather than a single attribute. Like its umbrella neighbour, it often marks an unwillingness to commit to a specific descriptor.

definition.beginner: Thick, dark, faintly bitter cane syrup with a mineral edge.
definition.expert: The darkest point of the caramelisation range, carrying bitterness and mineral depth alongside the sweetness.

references.name: Blackstrap molasses, or Indian sugarcane kakvi
references.prep: Half a teaspoon in a covered cup, smelled at room temperature. Treacle and golden syrup are lighter and sit closer to caramel.

definition.beginner: Woody, buttery sap boiled down — thinner and more aromatic than cane.
definition.expert: Distinguished from cane-derived sweetness by a woody, faintly resinous top note and lower viscosity of impression.

references.name: Pure maple syrup, dark grade
references.prep: Half a teaspoon in a covered cup. Maple-flavoured pancake syrup is fenugreek and caramel - it smells like the idea of the reference rather than the reference.

definition.beginner: Sugar taken just past melting: toasty, faintly bitter, deeply aromatic.
definition.expert: Mid-range caramelisation. Sits directly on the boundary with roast character, and which word a taster reaches for is usually decided by roast level.

references.name: White sugar, caramelised dry
references.prep: Melt a teaspoon of sugar in a dry pan until it turns amber, then take it off the heat before it darkens further and let it cool in the pan. Stop at amber: pushed further it becomes burnt, which is a different category.

causes.note: A sugar-browning product; the continuum it shares with roast character has no sharp edge.

definition.beginner: Floral, waxy, slightly sharp sweetness straight from the comb.
definition.expert: Floral-sweet with a waxy body. The most origin-driven member of this group, and the least explicable as a roast artefact.

references.name: A mild single-flower honey - acacia or clover
references.prep: Half a teaspoon in a covered cup, room temperature. Avoid strong honeys such as buckwheat or eucalyptus: they carry their own floral and medicinal notes.

definition.beginner: Sweet, bright and juicy character the bean brought from the farm rather than from the roaster.
definition.expert: Origin-derived attributes, heavily modulated by processing and drying. High-value and high-variance: the category most affected by fermentation control.

causes.note: Intensity rises sharply with pulp contact during drying.

definition.beginner: Small, dark, sweet-tart soft fruit — jammy when ripe, sharp when not.
definition.expert: Anthocyanin-rich soft fruit character. Common in naturals and high-altitude washed lots; at high intensity it shades into ferment.

definition.beginner: Concentrated, sticky, sun-shrunk sweetness — sugar without the juice.
definition.expert: Dehydrated sugar character with reduced acidity. Converges with molasses at darker roasts, which is the usual source of confusion.

definition.beginner: The orchard and tropical group: stone, pome and pulpy sweetness that is neither small-and-dark nor sharp-and-zesty.
definition.expert: A catch-all spanning pome, stone and tropical character. Its breadth makes it the least diagnostic group in the category.

definition.beginner: Zesty, sharp and aromatic peel character with a clean, mouth-watering finish.
definition.expert: Peel and juice character driven by citric acidity plus terpene aromatics. The acid and the aroma are separable, and good tasters separate them.

definition.beginner: Deep, dark, jammy soft fruit with a faint floral edge and little sharpness.
definition.expert: Dark soft fruit with lower acidity and a floral top note. Distinguished from its bramble neighbour by depth rather than sharpness.

references.name: Blackberry preserve with no added flavouring
references.prep: Half a teaspoon in a covered cup at room temperature. Check the label for elderberry or apple juice concentrate, which many preserves use as a base.

definition.beginner: Bright, tart and slightly perfumed soft fruit; sharper and more delicate than the darker ones.
definition.expert: High-acid bramble character with pronounced perfume. Sharper and less dense than its dark neighbour.

references.name: Raspberry preserve, whole-fruit
references.prep: Half a teaspoon in a covered cup. Smell it beside the blackberry reference: these two are the sibling pair the scoring engine prices at 70, and most people cannot split them on the first attempt.

definition.beginner: Soft, round, faintly waxy dark fruit — sweet with almost no bite.
definition.expert: Round, low-acid dark fruit. Frequently a marker of extended fermentation in naturals rather than of origin, which is worth saying out loud.

references.name: Dried blueberries, or blueberry preserve
references.prep: Crush three dried berries, or half a teaspoon of preserve, and cover for five minutes.

causes.note: Often produced by extended pulp contact rather than by variety or terroir.

definition.beginner: Light, sweet red fruit with a faint green-stem note; fragrant rather than deep.
definition.expert: Fragrant red fruit with a green-stem facet. At higher intensity it slides toward the overripe boundary.

references.name: Strawberry preserve, whole-fruit
references.prep: Half a teaspoon in a covered cup. A jelly rather than a preserve is mostly sugar and pectin and smells of very little.

definition.beginner: Sticky sun-dried vine fruit, deep and slightly leathery.
definition.expert: Dehydrated vine fruit; the lighter of the two dried attributes, carrying less bitterness than its stone-fruit sibling.

references.name: Dark raisins, not golden sultanas
references.prep: Four or five raisins, torn open, covered for five minutes. Golden sultanas are sulphured and smell of it.

definition.beginner: Dark, syrupy dried stone fruit with a faint bitterness behind the sweetness.
definition.expert: Dehydrated stone fruit. Darker and more bitter than its vine-fruit sibling, and the closer of the two to molasses.

references.name: Pitted prunes
references.prep: Tear one open and cover for five minutes. The reference is the dark, cooked-fruit depth, not the sweetness.

definition.beginner: Sweet, fatty, faintly milky tropical flesh with a dry, fibrous edge.
definition.expert: Lactonic tropical character. Shares fatty sweetness with the kernel group, which is why it crosses that category boundary so readily.

references.name: Fresh coconut flesh, or unsweetened desiccated coconut
references.prep: A teaspoon in a covered cup. Sweetened desiccated coconut is a confectionery smell and will not serve.

definition.beginner: Sweet dark stone fruit with a faint marzipan note behind it.
definition.expert: Stone fruit with a benzaldehyde facet. Common in naturals; the marzipan note is what separates it from soft dark fruit.

references.name: Dried sour cherries, or cherry preserve
references.prep: Tear two dried cherries open and cover for five minutes. Glace cherries are almond essence and sugar - a different reference entirely.

definition.beginner: Sharp, jewel-bright, tannic red juice — sweet and astringent at once.
definition.expert: High-acid red fruit with tannic astringency, which is what separates it from the softer red fruits.

definition.beginner: Sharp tropical sweetness with an enzymatic, almost prickly edge.
definition.expert: High-acid tropical character with a bromelain-like bite. At intensity it becomes hard to separate from early ferment.

references.name: Fresh pineapple
references.prep: A small piece, covered, smelled at room temperature. Tinned pineapple loses the ester top note that makes this attribute recognisable.

definition.beginner: Musky, sweet vine juice with soft acidity and a faint skin note.
definition.expert: Vine fruit character. The sober end of a continuum whose far end carries alcohol, and the boundary is the presence of that lift.

definition.beginner: Crisp orchard sharpness — clean, watery-sweet, with a green snap.
definition.expert: Malic-driven pome character. The fruit face of an acid a grader would name directly; the same percept from the other side.

references.name: A green apple
references.prep: Cut a slice, leave it two minutes to begin oxidising, then smell. Two minutes is deliberate: the reference most coffees carry is a slightly oxidised apple, not a just-cut one.

definition.beginner: Soft, fuzzy-skinned stone fruit; floral, sweet and low in sharpness.
definition.expert: Lactonic stone fruit with floral lift. Rounder and less acidic than pome character.

references.name: Tinned peach in juice, not syrup
references.prep: A piece in a covered cup with a little of its juice. Tinned is the better reference here: it is consistent all year, where a fresh peach is only itself for a fortnight.

definition.beginner: Delicate, grainy-fleshed orchard sweetness with very little acidity.
definition.expert: Soft pome character. Lower in acid and more subtle than its crisp neighbour, and easily buried by roast development.

definition.beginner: Bitter-edged pink zest with a slightly resinous, mouth-drying finish.
definition.expert: Bitter citrus with naringin-like astringency — the most bitter and most drying member of the group.

references.name: A fresh grapefruit, pink or white
references.prep: Zest a little onto a saucer. The sulphurous edge under the citrus is the part that distinguishes it from orange, and it is the part that survives into a cup.

definition.beginner: Round, sweet zest with soft acidity and a warm peel aroma.
definition.expert: Sweet citrus with lower acidity than the sharp members; the most approachable of the group and the least diagnostic.

references.name: A fresh orange
references.prep: Zest a little onto a saucer. Squeeze the peel to spray the oil if the zest smells thin.

definition.beginner: Clean, sharp, mouth-watering zest — bright without much sweetness.
definition.expert: High citric expression with clean zest aromatics. The usual reference point for the acid itself.

references.name: A fresh lemon
references.prep: Grate a little zest onto a saucer and smell within a minute. Zest, not juice: the juice is the acid reference, the peel oil is the aroma one.

definition.beginner: Sharp zest with a green, faintly bitter edge; more aromatic than sweet.
definition.expert: Sharp citrus with a green terpene facet that distinguishes it from its yellow neighbour.

references.name: A fresh lime
references.prep: Zest a little onto a saucer and smell immediately. Lime oil fades faster than lemon - grate it last if you are running several citrus references in one session.

definition.beginner: Sharpness, and the products of pulp breaking down — from clean brightness through to boozy, over-processed intensity.
definition.expert: Spans desirable organic acidity and process-derived attributes. The category where description and quality judgement most often diverge.

causes.note: Uncontrolled pulp contact pushes the whole category from the bright end toward the boozy end.

definition.beginner: The sharp, mouth-watering sensation itself, named as a sensation rather than as a fruit.
definition.expert: Organic acid attributes named by compound rather than by fruit reference. The Q exam tests these directly, and naming them is a distinct skill from naming fruit.

definition.beginner: Boozy, yeasty, over-ripened character from pulp left to break down too far — or deliberately.
definition.expert: Ethanol and ester-driven attributes. Stylistic under controlled anaerobic processing, a fault when uncontrolled — the sensory evidence is identical either way.

causes.note: Extended or uncontrolled fermentation; intent does not change the percept.

definition.beginner: A general sharp, tangy smell with no particular compound you can name.
definition.expert: An umbrella sharpness used when the specific organic acid cannot be identified. Like other umbrella terms, worth pushing a taster past.

definition.beginner: The sharp, nose-tingling smell of vinegar.
definition.expert: Vinegar character. In small amounts it lifts and brightens; in quantity it is the leading edge of a ferment fault.

references.name: White distilled vinegar
references.prep: One part vinegar to twenty parts water. Smell and taste. At full strength it will scour your nose for the rest of the session.

causes.note: Acetic bacteria during fermentation; the first marker to appear as control slips.

definition.beginner: Rancid dairy — the sour smell of butter left out far too long.
definition.expert: Rancid butterfat character. A definitive over-fermentation marker, and frequently mislabelled as animalic by untrained panels.

references.name: Butter left out to go rancid
references.prep: Leave a teaspoon of unsalted butter uncovered at room temperature for three days, then cover and smell. Unpleasant, and that is the reference - this is what over-fermentation smells like in a cup.

causes.note: Anaerobic bacterial activity past the useful window.

definition.beginner: Sweaty and cheesy — old socks, or a strong washed-rind cheese.
definition.expert: Sweaty, cheesy character from over-fermentation. Shares its cause with the rancid-dairy marker and usually appears alongside it.

causes.note: Over-fermentation; typically co-occurs with butyric character.

definition.beginner: Clean, sharp brightness of the kind that makes the mouth water — the sensation under lemon and lime.
definition.expert: The dominant acid in citrus. Clean and mouth-watering; distinguished from malic by lacking the green pome facet.

references.name: Food-grade citric acid - sold as nimbu ka phool in India, as a preserving acid elsewhere
references.prep: 0.5 g in 100 ml of water at room temperature. Taste, do not smell: this is a basic taste and it has almost no aroma. Make it fresh each session.

definition.beginner: Crisp green sharpness, like biting a tart apple.
definition.expert: The dominant acid in pome fruit. Green and crisp, and the acid most often reported as a fruit rather than as a sensation.

references.name: Food-grade malic acid, from a brewing or winemaking supplier
references.prep: 0.5 g in 100 ml of water. Taste it against the citric acid solution at the same concentration - side by side is the only way this pair teaches anything, and citric-versus-malic is the confusion the curated table exists for.

definition.beginner: Sweet vine fruit with a warm boozy lift behind it.
definition.expert: Vine character with ethanol lift. The boundary with plain vine fruit is the presence of alcohol and acetic top notes, not the fruit itself.

references.name: A dry red wine
references.prep: 10 ml in a covered glass, left five minutes. Use something plain and young; an oaked or aged wine brings vanilla and leather that belong to other wedges.

definition.beginner: Warm, oaky spirit character with vanilla and caramel behind the burn.
definition.expert: Barrel-aged spirit character: ethanol with oak lactones. Rare, and usually stylistic rather than faulty.

references.name: A blended whisky
references.prep: 5 ml in a covered glass. Smell across the rim rather than into the glass - ethanol at full strength numbs the nose for several minutes.

definition.beginner: Pulpy, yeasty, slightly sour funk — fruit that has begun to turn.
definition.expert: Uncontrolled pulp breakdown. Sought after in some modern processing and disqualifying in a washed lot; the cup cannot tell you which was intended.

references.name: Unflavoured kombucha, or the brine from naturally fermented pickles
references.prep: 10 ml in a covered cup. This is the attribute Defect Lab flags as context-dependent, so smell it with that in mind: the question is never whether it is present but whether it is in a coffee that wanted it.

causes.note: Extended pulp contact, wet weather during drying, or deliberate tank fermentation.

definition.beginner: Fruit a day or two past its best: heavy, sweet, and starting to go.
definition.expert: The transition point between desirable fruit and ferment, and the most common split-the-table call on a cupping table.

references.name: A banana left until the skin is fully black
references.prep: Smell the intact fruit, then peel it and smell again. Four or five days past ripe at room temperature gets you there.

definition.beginner: Fresh plant character: leaf, stalk, pod and sap, running from bright and living to dry and cured.
definition.expert: Chlorophyll and aldehyde-driven plant attributes. Usually a marker of under-ripe cherry or under-developed roast rather than of origin.

causes.note: Under-development leaves plant aldehydes intact; picking unripe cherry produces the same family from a different cause.

definition.beginner: Smooth, fatty, faintly peppery pressed-fruit character with a leafy edge.
definition.expert: Fatty, peppery character. Rare, and more often registered as a texture impression than as an aroma.

references.name: Extra-virgin olive oil, a freshly opened bottle
references.prep: 5 ml in a covered cup, warmed in the hand. A bottle open for months has gone flat and stale, which teaches the wrong attribute.

definition.beginner: Unfinished and starchy, as though the heat never quite got into it.
definition.expert: Under-development in the roast rather than in the fruit. Separated from immaturity by cause, not by sensation - which is why the two are so often confused.

causes.note: Insufficient heat penetration; the bean is cooked outside and raw within.

definition.beginner: The living-plant band: leaf, stalk, pod and cut stem.
definition.expert: The core plant group. Its members differ mostly in freshness and in how dried-out they read, not in kind.

definition.beginner: Starchy, dull legume character, like the water from a tin of pulses.
definition.expert: Cooked legume character. Almost indistinguishable from fresh pod character and, like it, a marker of under-development.

references.name: Dry raw kidney beans or chickpeas
references.prep: Crush a tablespoon coarsely and cover for five minutes. Raw and dry: cooked or tinned beans smell of the cooking, not the legume.

definition.beginner: Picked too early: hard, sharp, grassy and lacking sweetness.
definition.expert: Immature cherry character. Distinguished from roast under-development by the accompanying sharpness and astringency.

causes.note: Strip-picking or careless selection bringing immature cherry into the lot.

definition.beginner: The bright snap of a freshly split legume casing.
definition.expert: Fresh legume character, aldehyde-driven. The freshest member of the plant group and the least unpleasant.

references.name: Fresh peas in the pod
references.prep: Snap two pods open and cover for two minutes. Frozen peas will not serve: the aroma is in the pod, not the pea.

definition.beginner: Living, watery, just-cut plant smell — cool rather than dry.
definition.expert: Cut-plant aldehydes at low intensity; the most pleasant expression available in this group.

references.name: Freshly cut grass
references.prep: A pinch of clippings, bruised between the fingers, smelled within a minute. The compound responsible fades fast, so this reference has to be made rather than stored.

definition.beginner: Deep leafy character, like raw spinach or chard.
definition.expert: Concentrated chlorophyll character; heavier and less bright than cut-plant notes.

references.name: Raw spinach leaves
references.prep: Bruise three leaves and cover for two minutes.

definition.beginner: Cooked plant matter — the water left in the pan after boiling greens.
definition.expert: Cooked plant character; duller and more sulfurous than the fresh members of the group.

definition.beginner: Dry, dusty, sun-cured grass — warm and faintly sweet, with all the moisture gone out of it.
definition.expert: Dried grass character. Sits on the boundary with chamomile, and old-crop lots frequently show it alongside woodiness.

references.name: Hay or dried grass, from a pet shop or a field edge
references.prep: A small handful in a covered container. Keep it dry - damp hay turns musty, which is a fault in a different category.

causes.note: Ageing in storage as well as drying conditions at origin.

definition.beginner: Aromatic leafy sharpness — mint, thyme or sage rather than grass.
definition.expert: Aromatic herbaceous character with terpene lift, distinct from the flat green of cooked plant matter.

references.name: Fresh coriander leaf
references.prep: Bruise two leaves and cover. Substitute flat-leaf parsley if coriander reads as soapy to you - that is a genuine genetic difference and not worth training against.

definition.beginner: The remainder: staling, storage damage, taints, and the basic tastes that fit nowhere else.
definition.expert: A heterogeneous category holding most of the fault vocabulary plus two basic tastes. Where cupping most needs precision and usually gets least.

definition.beginner: Age, damp and storage: flat, dry, boxy and cellar-cold character.
definition.expert: Staling and storage attributes. The group most diagnostic of green handling and age rather than of roast or origin.

causes.note: Time, moisture and poor storage; almost never a roasting problem.

definition.beginner: Sharp, synthetic, medicine-cabinet and workshop smells, plus plain bitterness and saltiness.
definition.expert: Taints and basic tastes. Membership is defined by cause rather than by any shared sensory quality, which makes it the least coherent group on the wheel.

definition.beginner: Flat and lifeless — the aromatics have simply gone.
definition.expert: Loss of volatiles through age. The earliest and mildest point on the staling continuum.

definition.beginner: Dry, flat and faintly fatty, like a damp packing box drying out.
definition.expert: Lipid oxidation product. Further along the staling continuum than simple flatness, and the point at which most drinkers notice.

references.name: Corrugated cardboard
references.prep: Tear a piece to expose the fluting, breathe on it or mist it very lightly, and smell. The tear matters - a cut edge gives up much less.

definition.beginner: Dry, thin and dusty, like the inside of an old book.
definition.expert: Dry oxidised character without the fatty note of its cardboard neighbour.

references.name: An unrinsed paper filter
references.prep: Smell a dry filter, then pour 50 ml of hot water through one and smell the water. This is the reference that explains why rinsing the filter is not superstition.

definition.beginner: Dry, hollow, old-timber character with the sweetness gone out of it.
definition.expert: Old-crop marker. Frequently reported as tobacco, which arrives from the roast rather than from storage - a useful diagnostic split.

references.name: Pencil shavings or a wooden coffee stirrer
references.prep: A pinch of fresh shavings in a covered cup. Cedar pencil is the cleanest version of this.

causes.note: Extended green storage; the classic past-crop signature.

definition.beginner: Wet cellar and mildew — the smell of something stored badly.
definition.expert: Fungal growth from excess moisture in storage. A fault at any intensity, and a food-safety concern at high ones.

definition.beginner: Shut-up-room air with a fine powder note.
definition.expert: Dry storage taint without fungal wetness; distinguished from its earthy sibling by the absence of soil character.

definition.beginner: Damp soil and cellar floor — wet ground rather than dry powder.
definition.expert: Geosmin-driven soil character from damp storage. The wet counterpart to dusty staling.

references.name: Damp soil from a pot plant
references.prep: A teaspoon of moist soil in a covered cup. Potting compost, not garden soil with roots and leaf litter in it.

definition.beginner: Hide, wet fur and barnyard — warm and faintly sour.
definition.expert: Barnyard character. Overlaps heavily with the sweaty and rancid organic acids, which have an entirely different cause.

definition.beginner: Savoury and warm, like stock or a butcher's counter.
definition.expert: Savoury umami character. Contextual: at low intensity it reads as body and depth, at high intensity as a fault.

definition.beginner: Antiseptic and sharp — a hospital corridor, or a freshly opened plaster.
definition.expert: A serious fault, usually from bacterial contamination or specific agronomic problems. Shares an eugenol-adjacent family with clove, which is why the confusion is legitimate.

references.name: Dettol antiseptic liquid, or any chloroxylenol disinfectant
references.prep: One drop on a strip of filter paper. Phenolic is the fault most likely to be described as simply bad by someone who cannot name it, which is precisely why it earns a reference.

definition.beginner: One of the basic tastes: the drying, sharp sensation at the back of the tongue.
definition.expert: A basic taste, not an aroma. Excess usually indicates over-extraction or dark roast rather than a green defect.

references.name: Tonic water, left open until flat
references.prep: 50 ml at room temperature, tasted. The quinine is the bitterness; flat tonic removes the carbonation that otherwise reads as acidity.

definition.beginner: One of the basic tastes: a mineral, saline edge.
definition.expert: A basic taste. Rare in coffee; when present it usually points at brewing water or under-extraction rather than the bean.

references.name: Table salt
references.prep: 1 g in 100 ml of water. Taste only. Worth making once at this concentration so you know what a genuinely saline cup tastes like rather than guessing at it.

definition.beginner: Sharp and clinical — antiseptic, iodine, a first-aid box.
definition.expert: Clinical taint, near-synonymous in practice with phenol. Tasters reach for this word first and the diagnostic term second.

references.name: Iodine tincture, or a crushed soluble aspirin
references.prep: One drop of tincture on filter paper, or a crushed tablet in a covered cup. Iodine is also the rioy reference, and the overlap is real rather than sloppy.

definition.beginner: Fuel and solvent — a filling station forecourt.
definition.expert: Hydrocarbon taint, usually from contaminated storage or transport rather than from anything at the farm.

definition.beginner: Sulfurous and sharp, like a struck match or a gas leak.
definition.expert: Sulfur compound taint. Distinct from the softer cooked-plant sulfur of the vegetative group by its sharpness.

definition.beginner: Hot tyres and elastic bands — a burnt synthetic smell.
definition.expert: Common and characteristic in some robusta, where it is not a fault at all. Context decides, which makes it a good test of a taster's judgement.

references.name: A new rubber band, or an inner-tube patch
references.prep: Two or three bands in a covered cup, warmed in the hand for a minute. Warmth is what makes rubber give anything up.

definition.beginner: Warm, sharp and aromatic seasoning character — sweet-warm at one end, biting at the other.
definition.expert: Spans trigeminal pungency and sweet aromatic seasoning, which have little in common perceptually. Rarely dominant; usually a supporting note.

definition.beginner: A sharp physical bite in the nose and throat rather than a smell.
definition.expert: Trigeminal irritation without a defining aroma. Perceived as sensation rather than scent, which is why it resists description.

references.name: Fresh ginger root
references.prep: Grate a little onto a saucer. The reference is the sharp, penetrating quality that seems to reach the back of the nose, not the flavour.

definition.beginner: Dry, woody heat with a sneeze-provoking sharpness.
definition.expert: Piperine-driven character with woody top notes; distinguished from generic pungency by having an identifiable aroma.

references.name: Black peppercorns
references.prep: Crack three or four and cover for a minute. Freshly cracked - the aroma is largely gone from pre-ground pepper.

definition.beginner: The warm baking group: sweet, woody, faintly resinous seasoning.
definition.expert: Sweet aromatic seasoning. Members share warmth and differ mostly in sweetness and volatility.

definition.beginner: Sweet liquorice warmth with a cooling finish.
definition.expert: Anethole-driven sweet seasoning. The cooling facet is what separates it from the other warm spices.

references.name: Star anise, or fennel seed
references.prep: Crush one point of a star, or a pinch of fennel, and cover. Both carry anethole, which is the compound the attribute is really about.

definition.beginner: Dry, dusty, faintly woody warmth with a bitter edge.
definition.expert: Dry, resinous warmth. The least sweet member of the warm seasoning group.

references.name: A whole nutmeg
references.prep: Grate a little onto a saucer and smell fresh. Pre-ground nutmeg is largely gone within weeks of grinding.

definition.beginner: Sweet bark warmth, dry and slightly sharp.
definition.expert: Cinnamaldehyde character. Frequently a roast artefact rather than an origin note, particularly at lighter development.

references.name: A cinnamon or cassia quill
references.prep: Scrape the inner surface with a knife and smell the scrapings. Most of what is sold as cinnamon in India and North America is cassia - blunter and more medicinal than true Ceylon cinnamon. Either serves as a reference as long as you know which one you have.

causes.note: Often produced in the drum rather than carried from the farm.

definition.beginner: Intense sweet-warm bud character with a numbing, faintly antiseptic edge.
definition.expert: Eugenol-driven. The pleasant expression of the compound family that reads as a serious fault when it dominates.

references.name: Whole cloves
references.prep: Crush one and cover for a minute. Powerful enough to dominate a session, so smell it last.

definition.beginner: Perfumed, delicate blossom and dried-petal character.
definition.expert: Terpene and ester-driven blossom attributes. High-value, fragile, and the first thing lost to roast development.

causes.note: Destroyed by development; a dark roast cannot show this category at all.

definition.beginner: Dry, tannic, faintly perfumed leaf infusion with a drying finish.
definition.expert: Tannic infusion character with floral lift. Astringency is what separates it from the blossom notes proper.

references.name: Unflavoured black tea, a good loose leaf
references.prep: Smell the dry leaf, then steep 2 g in 100 ml just off the boil for three minutes and smell the surface. A plain Assam or Ceylon; anything bergamot-scented is a different reference.

definition.beginner: The blossom group itself: sweet, perfumed and delicate.
definition.expert: Blossom attributes proper. Members differ in sweetness, weight, and how quickly they fade from the cup as it cools.

definition.beginner: Soft, sweet, faintly dried-grass flower infusion.
definition.expert: Dried flower character sitting directly on the boundary with cured grass - a defensible confusion rather than an error.

references.name: Dried chamomile flowers
references.prep: Open a tea bag or use loose flowers, a teaspoon in a covered cup. Smell it against the hay reference: chamomile sits right on that boundary and the pair is a genuinely hard discrimination.

definition.beginner: Sweet, heavy, unmistakably perfumed petal character.
definition.expert: Geraniol and phenethyl alcohol driven; heavier and sweeter than the other blossoms.

references.name: Dried rose petals, or food-grade rose water
references.prep: A pinch of petals in a covered cup, or one drop of rose water on filter paper. Rose water is widespread in India as gulab jal and is the more consistent of the two.

definition.beginner: Intense, sweet, slightly green white-flower perfume.
definition.expert: Indole-containing white blossom. The most intense floral, and the one most often paired with leaf-infusion character.

references.name: Jasmine-scented green tea, dry leaf
references.prep: Smell the dry leaf in a covered cup. Scented tea rather than jasmine flowers: the flower is seasonal and the tea is the same every time, which is what a reference standard has to be.
